food.text: Millet was growing wild in Greece as early as 3000 BCE. It was one of the grains found in the landscape at the very start of the Bronze Age.
The Minoans of Crete traded extensively, exporting agricultural products and luxury crafts. In return they got raw metals, which were difficult to obtain on their island.

Linear B tablets found at Knossos, an important Mycenaean administrative centre after about 1450 BC, record administrative control over land, labour, livestock, textiles and offerings. They are a major source for studying how Late Bronze Age Crete was run.
Bulk storage containers for millet have been found from the Late Bronze Age in Macedonia and northern Greece. They show that the grain was kept in large quantities and not just gathered wild.
Pheasants were present in Greece as early as 2000 BCE. They belonged to a much wider range of birds that ancient Greeks ate than is typical today, and pheasants were later sold in markets.

art.text: Aegean art (2800–1100 BC) is sometimes called Greek Bronze Age art, but it covers three very different cultures. Cycladic art is known for simple figurines carved in white marble, Minoan art for palace frescos, bull-leaping imagery and sophisticated pottery and jewellery, and Mycenaean art for lavish gold metalwork, imagery of combat, and massively-constructed citadels and tombs.

Minoan art is described as elegant, rhythmic and full of movement. Between 2000 and 1700 BC its pottery was defined by technical perfection and dynamic swirling ornament, and many murals and reliefs showed animals, birds and sea creatures in lush vegetation, with marine life especially favored.

Depictions of boxing and bull-leaping in Greek art go back to the Bronze Age. The Minoans practiced wrestling, bull jumping, acrobatics and boxing, and these sports appear in art ranging from frescoes to pottery.

The Minoans were a Bronze Age Aegean civilization on Crete and other Aegean Islands that flourished from c. 3000 BC to c. 1450 BC. Their palace at Knossos had two to three levels, over 500 rooms, and many terraces with porticos and stairs.

The Minoans built several great palaces, most notably Knossos, Phaistos and Malia. They were destroyed around 1700 BC and rebuilt, then suffered some destruction again around 1500 BC. The rebuilt "new" palaces are the main source of information on Minoan architecture.

Mycenaean art is most prominently dated between 1600 and 1100 BC, during the Late Helladic period of Greece. Pottery is by far the most common type of Mycenaean art to survive, and it was often exported to Italy. The Warrior Vase is an unusually fine vase with painted figures.

Aegean artists worked in many materials, including stone, ivory, gold, silver, copper, bronze and clay. Very little trace of large free-standing sculpture has been found, but many examples of smaller sculptors' work exist. Vases were made in enormous number and variety, richly ornamented with colored schemes.

Many art historians consider the term "Aegean art" inappropriate, because it reflects geographic proximity rather than cultural or artistic unity. Others point to shared traits, especially after the "process of Minoanization from c. 1700 upwards", and to the difficulty of telling whether excavated objects were imported or made locally.

Minoan figures were painted as slim-waisted and athletic, and males and females differed only in skin color, with females shown lighter. Most images were flat and silhouetted against solid color backgrounds, so forms seem to float or sway.

The palace of Knossos, called the Palace of Minos, is the most elaborate and ambitious of the Minoan palaces. It is characterized by a vast number of rooms spread over a large amount of land, and it has been excavated and partially restored.

From about 2500 BC, Cretan metalworkers made vessels including cauldrons, pans, hydrias, bowls, pitchers, basins, cups and ladles. The earliest were probably made only from precious metals, and bronze versions came later.

Aegean artists engraved objects in great number, such as ring-bezels and gems, and an immense quantity of clay impressions was taken from these engravings. Early intaglios of this kind were called Inselsteine, and it was not until 1878 that C. T. Newton showed they were not stray Phoenician products.

The youth of the boys in the Akrotiri Boxer Fresco hints that Minoan athletes began training very early in life. It has been suggested that athletics played a religious role, and that competition may have been a rite of passage into adulthood for the Minoans.

Inscribed stirrup jars were oil flasks with stirrup-shaped handles, imported from Crete around 1200 BC. Carl Blegen noticed they matched jars Arthur Evans had dated to about 1400 BC, which led scholars to question Evans's date for the Knossos archive.

war.text: The Late Bronze Age collapse, in the late 13th to early 12th century BC, was sudden, violent and culturally disruptive across the Eastern Mediterranean, including the Aegean and the Balkans. In Greece, destruction was heaviest at palaces and fortified sites, and none of the Mycenaean palaces survived, with the possible exception of the fortifications on the Acropolis of Athens. Thebes had its palace sacked repeatedly between 1300 and 1200 BC and was eventually destroyed completely by fire. Up to 90% of small sites in the Peloponnese were abandoned, which suggests a major depopulation.

Mycenaean Greece introduced several innovations in engineering, architecture and military infrastructure. Its centers of power included Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns and Midea in the Peloponnese, along with Thebes and Athens in Central Greece.

During the reign of the Hittite king Hattusili III, the king of Ahhiyawa was recognized as a Great King. That made him equal in status to the rulers of Egypt, Babylonia and Assyria, so a power based around the Aegean stood among the top rulers of its age.

Around 1200 BC the palace centers and outlying settlements of the Mycenaean culture began to be abandoned or destroyed. By 1050 BC recognizable features of the culture, such as the Linear B script, had disappeared.

The palace economy of Mycenaean Greece and the Aegean disintegrated in the collapse. At Pylos, fire destroyed the city around 1180 BC, and Mycenae was wrecked by a series of major fires in 1190 BC. Up to 90% of small sites in the Peloponnese were abandoned. What followed was the small, isolated village cultures of the Greek Dark Ages, from about 1200 BC to about 800 BC. Surviving cities such as Athens had an impoverished culture and little trade, and it took centuries to recover. Literacy fell severely.

Around 1400 BC, Hittite records mention the military activities of an Ahhiyawan warlord named Attarsiya. He attacked Hittite vassals in western Anatolia, including Madduwatta, and may be related to the mythic figure Atreus.

Since the 19th century, scholars have proposed competing causes for the Late Bronze Age collapse, most involving the violent destruction of cities and towns. Suggested causes include climate change, volcanic eruptions, droughts, disease and invasions by the Sea Peoples. One recent proposal is an early, now-extinct strain of bubonic plague brought from central Asia by the Sea Peoples or other migrating groups. Others point to crop failure and famine, including famines under Ramesses III that some Egyptologists blame on the Hekla 3 eruption.

In about 1315 BC, Arzawa, a Hittite vassal state, led an anti-Hittite rebellion and received support from Ahhiyawa. At the same time Ahhiyawa appears to have controlled a number of islands in the Aegean, which archaeological evidence also supports.

In the Iliad's catalogue of ships, Agamemnon himself gave Arcadia the ships for the Trojan war because Arcadia did not have a navy. Most Peloponnese regions are named in that catalogue, which suggests the division is very ancient and reaches back to Mycenaean Greece.

Archaeologist Jesse Millek has argued that trade in Mycenaean pottery ended around 1250 BC, before the destruction of about 1200 BC. On that view, the destruction around 1200 BC could not have caused the end of that trade.

literature.text: The first written script of Greece was Linear A, an undeciphered script used for the Minoan language of Crete. After it came Linear B, a syllabic script used for Mycenaean Greek, the earliest attested form of the Greek language. The oldest Mycenaean writing dates to about 1400 BC.

Linear B, the syllabic script of the Mycenaeans, offers the first written records of the Greek language. The earliest extant examples of ancient Greek writing date to about 1450 BC and are in this script.

Greek myths were most likely first spread by Minoan and Mycenaean singers in an oral-poetic tradition starting in the 18th century BC. Over time, the heroes of the Trojan War became part of the oral tradition of Homer's epic poems, the Iliad and the Odyssey.

The earliest surviving works of ancient Greek literature are the Iliad and the Odyssey, which date to the early Archaic period. They are set in an idealized archaic past that scholars link in some way to the Mycenaean era.

Mycenaean Greek, the form of the language written in Linear B, is dated to about 1400 to 1200 BC. It is the earliest of the periods into which Ancient Greek is roughly divided, and it came before the Dark Ages and the Archaic or Homeric period.
Linear B was found mainly in the palace archives at Knossos, Kydonia, Pylos, Thebes and Mycenae. The script disappeared with the fall of the Mycenaean civilisation in the Late Bronze Age collapse.

Homer's poetry was developed around the time the Greeks developed writing, yet it would have been composed orally. Homer was part of an existing tradition of oral poetry, and the first poet certain to have composed in writing was Archilochus, in the mid-7th century BC.

Homeric Greek is a literary form of Archaic Greek, derived mainly from Ionic and Aeolic, and used in the Iliad and the Odyssey. It differed significantly in grammar and pronunciation from Classical Attic.
The final collapse of Mycenaean civilisation appears to have occurred about 1200 BC. Iron replaced bronze, cremation replaced burial, and writing was lost.

Linear B, the script used to write Mycenaean Greek, was found mainly in palace archives at Knossos, Kydonia, Pylos, Thebes and Mycenae. The oldest Mycenaean writing dates to about 1400 BC, and the script disappeared with the fall of Mycenaean civilisation.

Mycenaean Greek, dated c. 1400 – c. 1200 BC, is treated separately from the later Ancient Greek language. This reflects its age and the very different nature of the material and of the type of scholarship required to study it.

Egyptian records mention a land called Danaya for the first time around 1437 BC, in the reign of Pharaoh Thutmoses III. Danaya has been equated with the Danaoi, the name of a mythical dynasty in the region of Argos, which Homer also used as a name for the Greek people.

Hesiod, a near contemporary of Homer, wrote the Theogony and the Works and Days. The Theogony gives the succession of divine rulers as a story of violence: Gaia persuades Cronus to castrate his father Uranus, and Cronus then snatches up and eats each of his own children, until Zeus makes him vomit them up and, with the Cyclopes' help, hurls Cronus and the Titans down into Tartarus. The Works and Days covers the succession of human ages and the origin of human woes, through the myth of Pandora, whose overturned jar spilled out all the best of human capabilities except hope. The poems also explain the origin of sacrificial practices.

science.text: Britain was the first region in Europe to fully switch its metalwork to tin bronze, in the period 2200-2100 BC. The Aegean, including Greece, followed much later, adopting full tin-bronze technology by around 1500/1300 BC. The Aegean Bronze Age itself began c. 3200 BC.

Very early commerce in the Aegean is shown by the spread of Melian obsidian over the whole area. Cretan vessels appear to have been exported to Melos, Egypt and the Greek mainland, and Melian vases eventually found their way to Crete.

Aegean ships shown on gems, gem-sealings, frying pans and vases had low free-board, masts and oars. The most detailed picture is the 'ship fresco' at Akrotiri on Thera (Santorini), preserved by the ash fall from the volcanic eruption that destroyed the town.

Linear B was a syllabic script used to write Mycenaean Greek, the earliest attested form of the Greek language. Its oldest writing dates to about 1400 BC. It was found mainly in palace archives at Knossos, Kydonia, Pylos, Thebes and Mycenae, and disappeared with the fall of the Mycenaean civilisation.

Chariot wheels in Scandinavia have four spokes, as in Mycenaean Greece and the Carpathian Basin. According to Maran, chariots probably originated in the entire zone between the Carpathian Basin and the Southern Ural, and spread southwards from there to Greece and the Near East.
The final collapse of the Mycenaean civilisation appears to have occurred about 1200 BC. Iron took the place of bronze, cremation took the place of burial of the dead, and writing was lost.
The first written script of Greece was Linear A, an undeciphered script used for writing the Minoan language of Crete. Linear B came after it, and predates the Greek alphabet by several centuries.
No traces of currency have come to light in the Aegean, apart from certain axeheads that were too small for practical use. Standard weights have been found, along with representations of ingots.

Analyses of skeletal material from the shaft graves at Mycenae indicate connections to the north. This lends some support to the idea that chariot technology spread south into Greece from the zone between the Carpathian Basin and the Southern Ural.

In 1866 quarrymen extracting pozzolana, a siliceous volcanic ash, for the Suez Canal works discovered primitive structures on Therasia. When the find was followed up in 1870 on Santorini (Thera), the geologist Ferdinand A. Fouqué somewhat arbitrarily dated the remains to 2000 BC from the eruptive stratum above them.

Archaeologist Jesse Millek has shown that trade in Mycenaean pottery ended around 1250 BC, before the destruction of around 1200 BC. That destruction therefore could not have caused the end of this trade.

politics.text: Mycenaean Greece, spanning roughly 1750 to 1050 BC, was the first advanced and distinctively Greek civilization on the mainland, built around palatial states. Its centers of power included Mycenae, Pylos, Tiryns, Thebes, Athens and Iolcos.

During the reign of the Hittite king Hattusili III, the king of Ahhiyawa was recognized as a "Great King". That put him on equal footing with the kings of Egypt, Babylonia and Assyria, the other top rulers of the Bronze Age world.

At its peak in 1350 BC, Mycenae's citadel and lower town held a population of 30,000. It was a military stronghold that dominated much of southern Greece, Crete, the Cyclades and parts of southwest Anatolia.

Egyptian records first mention a land called Danaya around 1437 BC, under Pharaoh Thutmoses III. An inscription from the reign of Amenhotep III lists its cities, and Mycenae, Nauplion and Thebes have been identified with certainty.

Around 1400 BC, Hittite records describe an Ahhiyawan warlord named Attarsiya attacking Hittite vassals in western Anatolia, including Madduwatta. Attarsiya is possibly related to the mythic character of Atreus.

Under Hattusili III, another anti-Hittite movement led by Piyama-Radu broke out with the support of the king of Ahhiyawa. Piyama-Radu caused major unrest and later invaded the island of Lesbos, which then passed into Ahhiyawan control.

philosophy.text: The religion of Mycenaean Greece (c. 1600–1100 BC) appears to have been the mother of the Greek religion. It shared many divinities later found in classical Greece, including Zeus, Poseidon, and Dionysus.

Minoan religion on Crete has been reconstructed almost entirely from archaeology, such as paintings, statuettes, ritual vessels, seals and rings, because there are no readable texts for most of the period. Its central deity is generally agreed to have been a goddess. Sacred symbols included the bull, the horns of consecration, the labrys double-headed axe, and possibly the serpent.

Mycenaean customs such as animal sacrifices and votive offerings survived into the Greek period. So did religious terms like theos (deity), hieros (holy man), nawos (temple), and temenos (land cut off and assigned for communal purposes).

Scholars once thought Minoan religion was not centred on massive public temples like those of Egypt and Mesopotamia. It is now thought that the Minoan palaces, and perhaps the smaller villas, were themselves the temples, with religious ritual as one of their main purposes. There were also rural peak sanctuaries and many sacred caves.

Mount Ida, the highest mountain on Crete, was sacred to the Titaness Rhea in Greek mythology. Its Idaean Cave is where, according to legend, the god Zeus was born. Other legends place his birthplace in Psychro Cave on the Lasithi Plateau.

The marble figures of Cycladic art are usually called "idols", but experts by no means agree that they had a religious function. Most known examples were removed illicitly from unrecorded contexts, which seem usually to have been burials. Their purpose remains uncertain.

John Chadwick noted that at least six centuries lie between the earliest Proto-Greek speakers in Hellas and the earliest Linear B inscriptions. During that time, their concepts and practices will have fused with indigenous pre-Greek beliefs and possibly with Minoan religion. The few offering lists naming gods as recipients reveal little about religious practice.

Until after the Mycenaean conquest around 1450 BC, no currently understood names for Minoan deities exist. Scholars also have no real idea how the Minoans thought of their gods or of the relationship between gods and devotees. Many fundamental questions about Minoan religious practice remain extremely uncertain.

The Linear B tablets are mostly lists and inventories, and no prose narrative survives, much less myth or poetry. Still, much can be gleaned from these records about the people who produced them and about Mycenaean Greece.

Evidence pointing to human sacrifice in Minoan religion has been found at three sites. At Anemospilia near Mount Juktas, a young man's skeleton lay trussed in a contracted position on a raised platform with a bronze dagger among his bones, and the discoloration of his bones suggests he died of blood loss. At the sanctuary complex of Fournou Korifi in south central Crete, fragments of a human skull lay in a room with a hearth and cooking equipment. At the "North House" at Knossos, children's bones bore cut marks. The subject remains controversial.

Thomas G. Palaima (2008) determined that Mycenaean religion shared common origins with other pre-Greek peoples, including the Minoans. Even so, he found that "key elements" of Minoan religious traditions and beliefs are either wholly absent or negligible among the Mycenaeans.

Bones found by Peter Warren at the Knossos North House date to Late Minoan IB, before the Mycenaeans arrived. They belonged to at least four children in good health, and bore signs that they were butchered the way the Minoans slaughtered sheep and goats, which suggests the children were sacrificed and eaten. Dennis Hughes and Rodney Castleden argue the bones were a secondary burial, where the dead are buried twice. The main weakness of that argument is that it does not explain the cuts and knife marks upon the bones.

culture.text: Mycenaean Greece was the last phase of the Bronze Age in ancient Greece, lasting from approximately 1750 to 1050 BC. It was the first advanced and distinctively Greek civilization on the mainland, with palatial states, urban organization, works of art, and a writing system. The most prominent site, Mycenae, gave the culture its name.

Inside the palace at Knossos were monumental reception halls, vast apartments for the queen and bridesmaids, and bathtubs with complete sewage and drainage systems. It also held food deposits, shops, theatres and sport arenas. The walls were built of high-quality masonry covered with highly decorated frescos.

Modern archaeologists call the Bronze Age on mainland Greece the Helladic period, after Hellas, the Greek name for Greece. Its first phase, the Early Helladic, c. 3200–2000 BC, was a time of prosperity with the use of metals and growth in technology, economy and social organization.

Egyptian records first mention a land called Danaya c. 1437 BC, during the reign of Pharaoh Thutmoses III. An inscription from the reign of Amenhotep III lists Danaya cities including Mycenae, Nauplion, and Thebes. The name has been equated with the Danaoi, a name Homer also used for the Greek people.
The Mycenaean Greeks introduced several innovations in engineering, architecture and military infrastructure. Trade over vast areas of the Mediterranean was essential for the Mycenaean economy.

The palace economy of Mycenaean Greece disintegrated in the Late Bronze Age collapse, in the late 13th to early 12th century BC. It turned into the small isolated village cultures of the Greek Dark Ages, which lasted from c. 1200 BC to c. 800 BC.
The Middle Helladic period, c. 2000–1700/1675 BC, faced a slower pace of development on the Greek mainland. Yet it saw the evolution of megaron-type dwellings and cist grave burials.

Archaeologist Jesse Millek has shown that trade in Cypriot pottery largely ended in 1300 BC, and trade in Mycenaean pottery ended in 1250 BC. Both stopped before the destruction around 1200 BC, so that destruction could not have caused either end.
